A mode of apprehending Dante that Jiang contrasts with analytic logic and formal exam-style reasoning.
The faculty Jiang says leads to truth and is necessary for entering Dante's vision of heaven.
The Christian thinker Jiang invokes to identify the student's God-centered answer as Augustinian.
Dante's long-lost love and guide through Paradise in Jiang's setup of the poem.
Jiang's word for Dante's structured understanding of the heavens and the universe.
Jiang's primary device for Dante: a contradiction that the reader must reconcile rather than dismiss.
Poetic compression, using very few words to describe a great deal.
A sentence or word holding multiple meanings at once.
Jiang's distinction between Dante as a historical person and Dante as protagonist or poetic speaker.
The poem's appeal to a pagan classical figure inside a Christian description of heaven, treated by Jiang as paradoxical.
The death of Jesus around the year 33, treated by Jiang as a distinct historical moment rather than something to be conflated with medieval Christendom.
The identity Jiang wants the room to name explicitly as central to Christian understanding of Jesus.
The capacity to change history rather than remain trapped in a cyclical world, which Jiang ties to Christ's redemptive action.
Jiang's term for a cyclical cosmos governed by recurrence like the seasons, without a decisive historical break.
A historical transformation Jiang says Dante's new understanding of Christianity helps bring into being.
Named alongside the Renaissance as an outgrowth of Dante's reinterpretive poetic project.
A mythic metamorphosis figure invoked in the read-aloud passage to describe Dante's internal transformation.
A sea-god metamorphosis simile used to name Dante's inner transformation after looking at Beatrice.
Invoked by Jiang as a philosophical authority for treating time and space as conditions tied to embodied sensation.
The spirit world where Jiang says time and space fall away and different universes coexist simultaneously.
A divine power Dante invokes, which Jiang interprets as a spirit whose possession would enable poetic speech.
Beatrice's name for the earthbound misconceptions Dante must shed before he can understand heaven properly.
Raised in class as the Christian mode tied to belief without evidence and deferred by Jiang to Dante's later treatment of Paul.
Presented by Jiang as an institutional control system useful inside the human subset of reality but inadequate for heavenly understanding.
The freer faculty Jiang contrasts with logic and treats as necessary for understanding God and the Divine Comedy.
The inner guide Jiang says readers should follow once they stop treating logic as the sole route to understanding.
Jiang's label for Dante's initial uncertainty about whether he is really in the new universe Beatrice has opened.
Jiang's name for Paradise as a realm beyond ordinary time and space whose celestial locations are metaphorical stations.
Defined here not as a finished perfection but as another journey and a place that continues to generate inquiry.
The universe's God-like structure, which Jiang treats as the governing pattern Dante is trying to understand.
Jiang's claim that differentiated rank or station persists even in heaven.
Beatrice's metaphor for creation as a vast order in which each nature moves toward a proper destination.
Jiang's shorthand for the burdens or moral conditions that determine ascent or descent, which he treats as self-acquired rather than divinely assigned.
The participant's and Jiang's explanation for how people end up with different moral weights through their own acts.
Raised here as the contrasting destination that must be explained if God is not a punitive allocator of souls.
Jiang's science-fiction image for God's constant effort to draw the human being toward him.
A student's explanation for salvation pressure: people remain burdened when they cannot release their own guilt.
Raised here as the question of whether movement toward God depends on our own orientation and attention rather than divine monitoring.
Jiang's name for the ultimate law of the universe: every movement toward or away from God comes from chosen desire and will.
The destination one approaches by welcoming God, contrasted with turning away through misuse of freedom.
Jiang's paired terms for the inner faculty through which free choice becomes action and orientation toward God.
Used here to argue that God's total power includes the choice to grant freedom of choice to humans.
The human likeness to God that one student offers as the reason people are given meaningful freedom.
The creation formula invoked to justify why humans would inherit agency analogous to divine action.
Used as the condition God supposedly does not want, because forced belief would empty human agency of meaning.
Dante's cosmic arrangement in which natural things follow their proper motion while humans can depart from it.
The distinctly human capacity Jiang keeps interrogating: the freedom to choose, stray, and therefore make goodness meaningful.
Used to name the interior motive that free action reveals and divine judgment could supposedly assess.
Jiang's answer for why free will exists: love proves itself by granting freedom rather than controlling behavior.
Named here as the direct analogue of parental freedom granted to a child and therefore as the sign of divine love.
Jiang's phrase for free will as the deepest structure of reality because it is the form divine love takes.
Expanded here into a noncoercive theology in which God supports rather than compels the human creature.

glossary_terms.term: tree of the knowledge of good and evil
glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Introduced as the Edenic problem that may complicate whether humans possessed meaningful free choice before the fall.
Jiang uses metaphor to describe Dante’s way of explaining the human place in the universe without pretending to literal scientific adequacy.
Named as the best way to understand God in this discussion: a force calling human beings back without coercing their response.
Here it is grounded in Eden as the already-present option to obey or disobey, not as something created only after the fall.
Used to describe Paradiso’s layered cosmos, where the first plane encountered is the moon.
Jiang’s phrase for the soul’s basic desire, which explains movement toward God in the canto.
Introduced as Dante’s first explicit lunar problem and as Jiang’s gateway from physical observation to metaphysical interpretation.
Beatrice’s image for the limits of reason when sense experience cannot reach the truth at issue.
Named by Jiang as a faculty that must take over when logic and science reach their boundary.
Contrasted with reason as the mode needed for realities that exceed material explanation.
Jiang’s name for reason’s core act: dividing reality into classes so it can be analyzed, simplified, and manipulated.
Used to define imagination as an additive faculty that can make leaps and build realities together instead of reducing them.
In this packet intuition is described both as whole-bodied, pre-conscious apprehension and as the best guide for Dantean truth.
Jiang’s name for the truths imagination can reach after logic has exhausted its material utility.
The initial rational explanation for apparent variation in lunar brightness, tied to differing thickness or reflectivity of matter.
Paired with imagination as the faculty that can see truth where logical analysis cannot.
Jiang’s framing for the moon passage, where metaphysical ascent includes an argument about scientific explanation.
Appears in the reading as the basis for different celestial powers, against any single density-based explanation.
The thought experiment Beatrice uses to show that a truly hollow moon would let sunlight show through during an eclipse.
Jiang's shorthand for the fallback claim that lunar dimness comes from deep recesses where light gets trapped rather than reflected.
Presented both in the text and by Jiang as the route by which a reader can test truth instead of submitting to authority.
Beatrice's practical demonstration that greater distance does not by itself produce dimmer reflected brightness.
Jiang's summary for the moon episode, where poetic ascent includes an argument conducted in the idiom of experiment and refutation.
Beatrice's promised new form of illumination after Dante's error has been stripped away.
Jiang's label for the educational process by which Beatrice leads Dante toward truth instead of simply asserting it.
The student's phrase for how truth-bearing writing remains legible across very long stretches of history.
Raised by a student as part of why Dante's work could circulate beyond elite or local audiences.
A student's rough phrase for poetic thinking that does not move by straightforward logic.
The student's phrase for the contingent surface details of a scene, contrasted with the deeper archetypal pattern underneath.
Used by a student to name the timeless structure of readers returning to Dante for knowledge and nourishment across ages.
For Jiang, what the heart can recognize as true across both past and future rather than only in one historical moment.
